sections.html:
Wilmington is Delaware's largest city and the seat of New Castle County, where the Christina River and Brandywine Creek meet before flowing into the Delaware River. It is about 33 miles southwest of Philadelphia. The 2020 count was 70,898 residents, well under the 1940 peak of 112,504, after Interstate 95 cut through neighborhoods in the 1950s and population fell for decades.

The city lists more than 50 named neighborhoods, from Center City, Riverfront and Quaker Hill to Wawaset Park, Brandywine Village and The Flats. It has nine historic districts and one conservation district, Forty Acres. A house inside one of them can face extra review for exterior changes, so ask the city before you start a repair meant to help a sale.

Mills and shipyards shaped the street grid, and many Wilmington houses are rowhouses or twins built for the people who worked in them. DuPont began making gunpowder near the Brandywine in 1802, and the neighborhoods that grew up around its mills still show it.

Older construction usually means plaster walls, original wiring, steam or hot water heat and basements that have seen water. Those are the items a buyer's inspector flags first, and they are also what makes a financed sale fall apart late in the process. Get a clear picture of each one before you list, and decide what you will repair, what you will price in and what you will disclose.

The Riverfront is a different case. It was once shipbuilding and manufacturing land and saw state-sponsored renewal beginning in the late 1990s. The 1.2 mile Riverwalk, the convention center and the ballpark anchor a market unlike the older residential blocks inland.

Flooding is the weather issue that most affects a Wilmington sale. In September 2021 the remnants of Hurricane Ida flooded hundreds of buildings and displaced dozens of families in the city. Delaware's floodplain engineer has noted that FEMA maps reflect historic risk and do not account for future climate change, and that most homeowners and renters policies do not cover flood damage.

  • Check the FEMA flood zone for your parcel before you set a price or a timeline.
  • Gather flood insurance claims, repair receipts and records of any drainage work for the buyer.
  • Expect inspectors to look hard at basements, sump pumps and foundation walls.
  • Tell buyers what you know. Delaware's seller disclosure law requires it, as covered below.

Wilmington bills city property tax, New Castle County sets the assessed value, and the school district adds its own tax. For fiscal year 2026 the city's rates are $3.7413 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $5.8276 per $1,000 for non-residential property. The city said these raise the same total revenue as the year before, and that its figures rest on the county's first countywide reassessment since 1983.

City bills go out in July with the city portion due September 30. County and school taxes come due November 30. Rates can change from one year to the next, so read the current bill on the city's property tax page before you do any math.

A senior exemption covers the first $210,300 of assessed value. Income limits apply, and applications are due May 16.

Taxes are normally prorated at settlement. If you have not paid the current bill, it is usually taken out of your proceeds.

Delaware's realty transfer tax is normally 4 percent of the value, made up of 2.5 percent for the state and 1.5 percent for the county or municipality. The statute divides it equally between seller and buyer. Wilmington also has its own transfer tax rules in Chapter 44, Article IV of the city code.

The city's exemption affidavit lists categories such as foreclosure, divorce, mortgage default, governmental transfers and parent and child. A first-time buyer exemption in the city requires that the buyer has held no legal interest in residential real estate in Wilmington for at least three years and intends to occupy the home within 90 days.

  • An attorney must conduct the settlement. The Delaware Supreme Court's 2000 Mid-Atlantic Settlement Services decision and a September 22, 2006 order treat closings as the practice of law.
  • Under 30 Del. C. 5402, a first-time buyer's share can drop by 0.5 percent of the first $400,000 of value, a reduction of up to $2,000. The seller's share stays the same.
  • Nonresident individual sellers must send estimated tax on the gain, 6.6 percent for individuals, with Form REW EST when the deed is presented for recording.

sections.h2: Rental licenses and vacant property fees
sections.html:
A rental in Wilmington needs a Residential Property Rental License, renewed each year under city code section 5-92, and a newly acquired rental is registered with the Department of Licenses and Inspections. Buyers and sellers may be asked for proof of the transaction. Inspections run on a two or five year cycle depending on the number of units.

If you inherited a house or the last tenant left, vacancy can cost more than people expect. The vacant property fee depends on how many years the property has stood vacant, no matter who owns it:

Years vacantAnnual fee
Less than 1$0
1$500
2$1,000
3 to 4$2,000
5 to 9$3,500
10$5,000, plus $500 for each year after

Owners must tell the department within 30 days of a sale or a change of mailing address. Failure to register can bring a fine of up to $500 or a civil action. Ask the city for a payoff figure early so no surprise lands at closing.

sections.h2: What a Wilmington seller must disclose
sections.html:
A seller of residential property with one to four units must put all known material defects in writing under the Buyer Property Protection Act. The Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report goes to buyers before they make an offer. Section 2572 calls for the disclosure before the listing agreement is signed, and for updates if something material changes before settlement.

Section 2577 exempts certain transfers: those under a court order in an estate, trust or guardianship, deeds in lieu of foreclosure, sheriff's sales, and transfers between co-owners or to a spouse or lineal relative. If you are selling as an executor or after a foreclosure filing, ask your attorney which side of that line you are on.

A cash sale drops the mortgage approval and appraisal, so closing can follow your schedule once title is clear. A traditional listing shows the house to more buyers but adds showings, repair requests and the chance that financing falls through.

Neither path avoids the attorney closing, the transfer tax split or the need to pay off city charges. We buy houses as-is, and we do not promise a price before we have seen the property. If an offer does not suit you, you owe nothing.

Before you decide, gather the deed, your latest tax bill, any rental license, flood or repair records and a written list of what you know about the house. With those in hand, you can compare a cash offer against a listing price on equal terms.

faqs.q: How much is the realty transfer tax when selling a house in Wilmington?
faqs.a: It is normally 4 percent of the property value, with 2.5 percent going to the state and 1.5 percent to the local government, and Delaware law divides it equally between seller and buyer. Wilmington has its own transfer tax rules in Chapter 44, Article IV of the city code, so confirm your exact figure with your closing attorney.

faqs.q: Do I need an attorney to sell my house in Wilmington?
faqs.a: Yes. Delaware requires an attorney to conduct real estate settlements, following the Delaware Supreme Court's 2000 Mid-Atlantic Settlement Services decision and its September 22, 2006 order.

faqs.q: When are Wilmington city property taxes due?
faqs.a: City bills go out in July, with the city payment due September 30 and county and school taxes due November 30. Check the city's property tax page for the current year's dates.

faqs.q: What happens if my Wilmington house has been empty for years?
faqs.a: The city charges a vacant property fee that grows with each year of vacancy, from $0 under one year to $5,000 at ten years, plus $500 for each extra year. The fee follows the property, so it continues even if ownership changes.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Wilmington house that has flood damage?
faqs.a: Yes, but you must disclose known material defects in writing under 6 Del. C. 2572. Gather repair records and insurance claims, since most homeowners policies do not cover flood damage.
